42855019.title: Outcomes among Patients with Single-Vessel Tibial Runoff Undergoing Revascularization for Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia, and the Role of Peroneal Communicating Branch Quality.
42855019.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Data evaluating outcomes among patients with single-vessel tibial runoff are limited. Our aim was to compare outcomes across patients with sole anterior tibial (AT), peroneal, or posterior tibial (PT) runoff following revascularization for chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), and to evaluate whether the quality of peroneal communicating branches affects outcome risk within the peroneal runoff population.

METHODS: All patients undergoing first-time revascularization for CLTI were retrospectively reviewed (2005-2022) and stratified by sole runoff vessel (AT, peroneal, PT). Primary outcomes were wound healing, major amputation, major adverse limb events (MALE), and amputation/death, assessed by Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression. A subset analysis stratified single-vessel peroneal runoff patients into a three-tiered, Peroneal Communicating Branch (PCB) Grade: Both branches present with at least one robust (PCB Grade 1), a single robust branch (PCB Grade 2), or no robust branch (PCB Grade 3), and compared each to the single-vessel AT/PT reference group.

RESULTS: Overall, 732 patients had single-vessel below-knee runoff: 225 AT, 315 peroneal, and 192 PT. Groups differed significantly in age, sex, and diabetes prevalence. Unadjusted two-year major amputation rates were significantly higher in the peroneal group (19% vs. 9.4% [AT] vs. 8.7% [PT]; P<.001), as were MALE rates (30% vs. 14% vs. 26%; P=.01). After adjustment, peroneal runoff was independently associated with higher risk of major amputation (HR 1.81 [1.04-3.13]) and MALE (HR 1.52 [1.03-2.25]) compared with AT/PT runoff. These associations persisted in the endovascular cohort (major amputation: HR 2.09 [1.06-4.13]; MALE: HR 1.59 [1.08-2.35]) but did not reach significance in the bypass cohort, which was limited by low event rates. When patients with single-vessel peroneal runoff were stratified by PCB Grades, unadjusted one-year major amputation rates followed a clear anatomically-driven pattern (6.9% (AT/PT) vs. 5.4% (PCB Grade 1) vs. 15% (PCB Grade 2) vs. 32% (PCB Grade 3); P<.001). After adjustment, when compared to AT/PT runoff, patients without any robust branch (PCB Grade 3) had significantly higher risk of major amputation (HR 3.21 [1.76-4.84]) and MALE (HR 2.41 [1.53-3.79]), while those with two branches with at least one being robust (PCB Grade 1) demonstrated higher rates of complete wound healing (HR 1.69 [1.09-2.62]) and no difference in major amputation or MALE.

CONCLUSIONS: Peroneal runoff is independently associated with worse limb outcomes following revascularization for CLTI, but this risk may be primarily driven by patients with absent or diminutive communicating branches. Those with robust branching demonstrate outcomes comparable to AT/PT runoff, underscoring the importance of further evaluation and pre-operative assessment of peroneal communicating branch quality - using the proposed PCB Grading system - in revascularization planning.

42854197.title: Incidence of Retinal Artery Occlusion After Carotid Endarterectomy Versus Carotid Artery Stenting.
42854197.abstract:
PURPOSE: Retinal artery occlusion (RAO) is a rare but vision-threatening complication of carotid revascularization, yet its comparative incidence after carotid endarterectomy (CEA) versus carotid artery stenting (CAS) is poorly characterized. We compared the risk of RAO and associated neurologic outcomes after CEA and CAS.

METHODS: Retrospective multicenter cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network (January 1, 2004-March 15, 2026). Adults undergoing CEA or CAS with ≥6 months of follow-up and no prior diagnosis of any studied outcome condition (retinal artery or vein occlusion, glaucoma, legal blindness, or stroke were included. Propensity score matching on demographics, comorbidities, ophthalmic conditions, medications, and laboratory biomarkers (nearest-neighbor greedy algorithm; caliper 0.25 SD) yielded 17,851 patients per cohort. The primary outcome was the incidence of RAO at 90 days and 1 year after the index procedure. Secondary outcomes included central RAO (CRAO), branch RAO (BRAO), retinal vein occlusion, glaucoma, legal blindness, stroke (stratified by National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale [NIHSS] score), and mortality at the same intervals. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated.

RESULTS: At 1 year, CAS was associated with higher risks of RAO (0.421% vs 0.257%; OR 1.64; 95% CI, 1.12-2.41), CRAO (OR 2.30; 1.10-4.84), BRAO (OR 3.21; 1.58-6.52), and legal blindness (OR 1.59; 1.26-2.92). CAS also conferred higher odds of stroke (6.20% vs 4.43%; OR 1.42; 1.25-1.62) and mortality (6.41% vs 3.87%; OR 1.70; 1.54-1.88). Most events occurred within 72 hours post-procedure.

CONCLUSION: In this retrospective propensity-matched analysis, CAS was associated with greater risk of retinal and neurologic ischemic complications than CEA, although absolute event rates were low. These observational findings support consideration of heightened postoperative ophthalmic vigilance and interdisciplinary collaboration between ophthalmology and vascular surgery after CAS and suggest that targeted post-procedural ophthalmic evaluation may be reasonable in selected high-risk patients, pending prospective confirmation.

42855613.title: Apixaban vs rivaroxaban for venous thromboembolism: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42855613.abstract: Direct oral anticoagulants are first-line therapy for venous thromboembolism (VTE), yet comparative evidence between apixaban and rivaroxaban remains limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of apixaban versus rivaroxaban in patients with VTE. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library was conducted from inception through March 2026. Studies directly comparing apixaban and rivaroxaban in adult VTE patients were included. Outcomes, including recurrent VTE, major bleeding, all-cause mortality, and net clinical harm, were pooled using a random-effects model. Thirteen studies comprising more than 220,000 patients were included. Apixaban was associated with a significantly lower risk of recurrent VTE compared to rivaroxaban (RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.74-0.98), with moderate heterogeneity. Apixaban was also associated with a significant 28% reduction in major bleeding risk (RR 0.72; 95% CI 0.65-0.81), with low heterogeneity, indicating consistent findings across studies. When efficacy and safety outcomes were combined, apixaban demonstrated a significantly lower risk of net clinical harm (RR 0.76; 95% CI 0.68-0.86). In contrast, no statistically significant difference was observed in all-cause mortality (RR 0.95; 95% CI 0.80-1.12), with substantial heterogeneity across studies. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings, with no single study significantly altering the overall estimates. Overall, apixaban demonstrated a more favorable efficacy and safety profile compared with rivaroxaban in VTE management, with reduced recurrence and bleeding risk, while mortality remained comparable. These findings suggest that apixaban may be associated with a more favorable efficacy and safety profile than rivaroxaban; however, the results should be interpreted cautiously given the predominance of observational evidence.
